results.summary: This design displays a fish sprite that bounces around a VGA screen, based on the VGA Playground logo example. It is used by connecting the chip to a VGA monitor and loading the project. The only external hardware required is a VGA display. The documentation is minimal and does not describe any testing or silicon results.

This design implements a side-scrolling 7-segment display with a programmable 16-character message memory. It is used by setting register-select switches to choose a memory location, setting character-encoding switches to the desired character, and toggling a write switch to load the character. An external board with an additional 7-segment display is required for full functionality. The documentation provides a character encoding table but no silicon test results.

This project is a basic three-body simulation using Manhattan distances and bucketed acceleration values, output to a VGA display. The documentation is essentially placeholder text and does not explain how to use or test the design. No external hardware is described. The design cannot be evaluated from the available information.

This design is a tiny system-on-chip with a 16-bit microprocessor, boot ROM, PWM, timer, and SPI interface. It is used by powering on the chip, after which the boot ROM runs a program that reads input from an 8-bit port and displays it on an 8-bit output port, while also exercising the SPI, PWM, and timer peripherals. External hardware such as a keypad, 7-segment display, or LCD is suggested but not finalized. The project is intended to test the microprocessor and peripherals on silicon, but no silicon results are reported.

This design reads RGB332 pixel data from a QSPI flash memory and displays it on a VGA screen, with configurable timing and latency. It is used by flashing an image to QSPI flash, setting configuration registers via a shift register interface, and enabling the display. External hardware includes a QSPI Pmod and a Tiny VGA Pmod. The design supports up to 720p and 1024x768 resolutions and allows switching between multiple images stored in flash.

This design implements a simplified version of the Chrome Dino game on a VGA display, where a dinosaur jumps over obstacles and cannot lose. It is used by connecting a button to input pin 0 and a VGA display to the outputs, then pressing the button to make the dinosaur jump. External hardware required includes a VGA display and a button with a power source. The documentation is brief and does not mention any testing or silicon results.

SotaSoC is a RISC-V 32-bit embedded system-on-chip with an RV32IC core and peripherals including SPI, I2C, UART, PWM, and GPIO. It is used by connecting a QSPI Pmod for program storage and optionally other peripherals like an ST7789 LCD, with software support for FreeRTOS and bare-metal. External hardware includes a QSPI Pmod, LEDs, and an optional SPI LCD. The design is notable for its configurability and support for FPGA prototyping, but no silicon test results are provided.

This design is an 8-bit CPU with a custom instruction set that relies on an external RP2008 microcontroller for RAM emulation. It is used by connecting the CPU's address and data buses to the RP2008, which provides memory and I/O. The documentation is a work in progress and directs users to the project repository for updates. No testing details or silicon results are available.

This design is a true random number generator based on three ring oscillators of different lengths, XORed together and debiased with a Von Neumann corrector. It is used by connecting a UART-to-USB adapter to read the 32-bit random numbers, and a dual-digit 7-segment display shows status; DIP switches control the oscillator speed. External hardware includes a UART adapter, a 7-segment display, and switches. The design outputs random numbers via UART and is notable for its ring-oscillator-based entropy source.

TinyScanChain is a low-footprint scan chain design for the IHP PDK, using custom cells built from standard cells to reduce area. It is used by connecting a microcontroller or CPU to the scan chain pins and clocking data in and out in bursts of 8 pulses per bit. External hardware includes a microcontroller, likely a Raspberry Pi, to drive the scan chain. The design is notable for its compact size and use of a simple SPI-like protocol, but no silicon results are reported.
